perPress.answerFull:
The paper uses fixed **sine and cosine** positional encodings, with each dimension cycling at a different frequency:

$$PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right)$$
$$PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right)$$

where `pos` is the token position and `i` indexes the embedding dimension. The wavelengths form a geometric progression from $2\pi$ up to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$.

The reason for picking sine and cosine is that this construction lets the model **learn relative positions easily**. For any fixed offset $k$, the encoding at position $pos+k$ can be written as a **linear function** of the encoding at $pos$, so attention heads can pick up on "distance $k$" relations with a simple learned linear projection. The fixed sinusoidal version performed nearly identically to learned positional embeddings in their ablation, so they kept the fixed one.

perPress.label: long-range-multihead-cost-rationale
perPress.answerPreview:
Here's the reasoning, straight from the section on Multi-Head Attention.

**The setup:** each head $i$ has its own projection matrices $W^Q_i, W^K_i, W^V_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}$, where $d_k = d_{\text{model}}/h = 64$ when $h = 8$. There's also a final output projection $W^O \
perPress.answerFull:
Here's the reasoning, straight from the section on Multi-Head Attention.

**The setup:** each head $i$ has its own projection matrices $W^Q_i, W^K_i, W^V_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}$, where $d_k = d_{\text{model}}/h = 64$ when $h = 8$. There's also a final output projection $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{h d_v \times d_{\text{model}}}$.

**Why the cost stays the same:**

In single-head attention with full dimension $d_{\text{model}}$, the projections are $W^Q, W^K, W^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}}$, so each one carries $d_{\text{model}}^2$ parameters and costs $O(d_{\text{model}}^2)$ to apply per token.

In multi-head, you replace those three big matrices with $h$ smaller ones of shape $d_{\text{model}} \times (d_{\text{model}}/h)$ each. The parameter count per projection becomes:

$$h \cdot d_{\text{model}} \cdot \frac{d_{\text{model}}}{h} = d_{\text{model}}^2$$

So the total projection work is unchanged. The heads run in parallel on smaller slices, and the concatenation through $W^O$ has the same shape as the original single output projection. Net cost of the projection step: identical.

**The attention computation itself** scales with $d_k$ per head. Since $d_k = d_{\text{model}}/h$, each head does less work, but you do $h$ of them in parallel, so the total comes out to roughly the same $O(d_{\text{model}}^2)$ as a single head running at full dimension. That's exactly the trade-off the section calls out: split the dimension, run more heads, keep the math equivalent.

In short, $\sum_i d_k = d_{\text{model}}$, so splitting the channel dimension across heads doesn't change how much work the Q/K/V projections or the final mixing have to do.

perPress.label: decoder-masking
perPress.answerPreview:
**Decoder self-attention** has one key difference from encoder self-attention: it's masked so each position can only look at earlier positions, not future ones. The encoder sees the whole sequence bidirectionally, but the decoder predicts left-to-right, so it has to be blocked from peeking ahead.

T
perPress.answerFull:
**Decoder self-attention** has one key difference from encoder self-attention: it's masked so each position can only look at earlier positions, not future ones. The encoder sees the whole sequence bidirectionally, but the decoder predicts left-to-right, so it has to be blocked from peeking ahead.

This is paired with the **offset-by-one trick**: input embeddings are shifted right by one position so position $i$ predicts token $i+1$. Together with the mask, that guarantees the prediction at any spot only depends on what came before it.

The decoder also has a third attention sub-layer (encoder-decoder cross-attention) on top of its two self-attention sub-layers, but that's separate from the self-attention difference you're asking about.

perPress.answerFull:
So this is the famous "Attention Is All You Need" paper. The short answer is yes, and the paper itself shows the first hint of that. The authors didn't just beat translation benchmarks, they also applied the Transformer to English constituency parsing, with both limited training data and a much larger semi-supervised setting of about 17M sentences, and it worked well there too.

The bigger reason people got excited, though, is what came after. That same architecture showed up in basically every major domain: vision (ViT), speech, protein folding (AlphaFold), and of course the GPT and BERT family. So the paper itself only demonstrates generalization to one extra task, parsing, but the strong opinion at the time, and what history has largely confirmed, is that yes, a fully attention-based stack generalizes very well beyond translation, mostly because self-attention is a flexible way to mix information across any sequence, whether the "sequence" is words, image patches, audio frames, or amino acids.
